newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD grapples with global trade, jobs, bribes.
newsitem.headline: OECD grapples with global trade, jobs, bribes.

text.p: Ministers from the 29 countries of the OECD met on Monday to renew a message of confidence in the economic benefits of increasingly global trade and to look for ways of selling "globalisation" better to the public.

The annual two-day meeting of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development is expected to finish with the now traditional declaration of support for budgetary and spending restraint across the OECD members' economies.

"Australia welcomes the OECD reports showing the need to continue structural reform" Australian trade minister Timothy Fischer told Reuters. His comments were similar to those of other ministers ahead of an end-of-day news conference.

A draft of the communique being prepared for release at the end of the two-day summit on Tuesday showed the ministers would endorse the trend towards ever more global trade and encourage member countries to keep cleaning up public finances and cutting spending to reduce budget deficits and debt.

"Ministers underlined their conviction that globalisation offers a real opportunity to improve living standards in their own countries and to allow all countries to participate in world development," says a copy of the draft obtained by Reuters.
"The challenge for governments is to pursue policies whereby the benefits of globalisation are fully realised while those most adversely affected are assisted," it says.

"OECD countries generally have budget deficit or debt levels which are still too high and population ageing threatens to push up public spending further," says the draft, which OECD sources say is unlikely to change much before formal release on Tuesday.
"Given high tax burdens in many countries, the main effort in cutting deficits will have to fall on expenditures," it says.

"Ministers noted that economic growth, projected to average 2.5 to 3 percent in 1997-98, seems likely to be more balanced across OECD countries. Inflation is low almost everywhere but unemployment remains high in many countries."
The draft showed ministers were also expected to signal their support for the creation of a single European currency.

Among other issues to be grappled with over the two days are a campaign against bribery in international business. Ministers are also due to sign an agreement with Russia on closer ties, holding out the prospect of OECD membership in the longer term.

U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley said on Friday night agreement had been reached on how OECD countries should start legislating to criminalise bribery of state officials in a bid to eliminate corruption from international business dealings.

The United States has been at loggerheads with France and Germany over how to tackle bribery but Daley told reporters in Washington a deal had been reached in which OECD states agreed to introduce laws by April 1998 and simultaneously start talks on a treaty which would achieve the same end.

The ministers are set to offer a "friendly-but-firm" signal on a Russian membership request, with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov arriving on Tuesday to sign an agreement opening direct cooperation channels with the OECD.

Highlighting the policy dilemmas involved at an organisation whose main goal is promoting a more "liberal" economic strategy is a report which shows structural unemployment has risen during the 1990s but which commends those who have reformed.

The report prepared for the meeting praises Ireland and the Netherlands for reducing structural unemployment, by cutting unemployment benefit and raising education levels in the first case and wage moderation and payroll tax cuts in the latter.
The report says overall unemployment among 23 of the 29 member countries -- the most recent members are not included -- rose to 7.7 percent in 1996 from 6.1 percent in 1990.

Structural unemployment, which strips out the portion of joblessness attributed to the ups and downs of the economic cycle, stood at 7.1 percent in 1996, versus 6.8 percent at the start of the decade, the report says.
